questions.question: A news bulletin reports that GDP reached a record high this year. Using the two measurement corrections from the lesson, explain why the average South African could still be worse off.
questions.expected_answer: First correct for prices: if the record is in nominal terms, part of the rise is inflation — real GDP at constant prices is the honest output measure (nominal up 7% during 6% inflation is only about 1% real growth). Then correct for people: divide real GDP by the population. South Africa's real growth of about 1% a year has run below population growth of about 1,5%, so real GDP per capita has been falling — total output at a record high while the average person's share shrinks. Both statements can be true at once because they use different measures.

questions.question: Construct the Lorenz curve in words — axes, the diagonal, the actual curve with a South African reading — and define the Gini coefficient, giving its endpoints and South Africa's approximate value.
questions.expected_answer: Axes: cumulative percentage of the population from poorest to richest along the horizontal; cumulative percentage of income up the vertical. The straight diagonal from bottom-left to top-right is the line of perfect equality — any share of people receives that same share of income. The actual curve runs corner to corner but droops below the diagonal: in South Africa the poorest 60% receive only about 10% of income, so the curve sits at 10 where the diagonal sits at 60. The deeper the droop, the greater the inequality. Gini = area between diagonal and curve divided by the whole area under the diagonal: 0 is perfect equality, 1 is one person holding everything; South Africa measures about 0,63 — the most unequal major economy reliably recorded.

questions.question: Name South Africa's four redistribution methods with one example each, then argue the growth-redistribution tension in both directions and state the lesson's conclusion.
questions.expected_answer: 1. Progressive taxation — income tax brackets stepping from 18% to 45%, with VAT zero-rating of staples softening regressivity. 2. Cash transfers — grants reaching about 28 million people monthly (older persons above R2 000, child support above R500, disability, SRD). 3. Redistribution in kind — free basic water and electricity, no-fee schools, feeding schemes, subsidised clinics, state housing. 4. Labour-market and asset measures — the national minimum wage, empowerment and land reform, and education spending that moves skills, tomorrow's earning power. Tension: redistribution spends what growth earns, and over-taxation can drive investment and jobs away; but a Gini of 0,63 also strangles growth because people without food, skills or transport can neither produce nor buy. Conclusion: growth and redistribution are complements — each funds and feeds the other.
